picked.t: Why some high-earning couples still struggle to save
picked.body: "The wedding was expected to cost VND200 million, but we couldn’t afford it. We had to pay deposits in stages and cut back on spending," the 31-year-old who lives in Ho Chi Minh City says. Before moving in with her boyfriend and having their family, she had lived with her parents and had to take care of few household expenses. Most of her earnings went toward travel. Peter, her British husband now, teaches in Vietnam and earns around VND80 million a month. He used to consider Ho Chi Minh City inexpensive and spent freely. Once they moved in together, rent alone cost more than VND20 million a month. They ate out several times a week, spending VND800,000 to over VND1 million per meal. She paid for their cat’s care, shopping, and a housekeeper hired by the hour. He covered the rent and household expenses, along with gym fees, sauna visits, and four or five trips a year. To save for the wedding, he swapped lunches costing nearly VND200,000 for free cafeteria meals at the school where he teaches. They also canceled all travel plans. For three months, he had felt as though his wings were clipped since he could no longer spend as he pleased. They have no immediate plans to have children because they consider their finances unstable. In Mekong Delta province of Vinh Long, Thu Nghiem and Van Sang, both 26, faced a similar problem. When they needed money to repair their house late last year, they discovered they had no savings despite earning more than VND40 million a month. They run a pizza shop, Sang also works as a real estate broker, they own their home, have no children or debts, and do not have to support their parents financially. Nghiem considered their income substantial for the area. "The fact that we hadn’t managed to save anything was difficult to accept," she says. They blamed each other and stopped speaking. They scaled back their plans to decorate and furnish the house, looking for cheaper alternatives, and had to borrow money from both families. "We realized that we had been spending money mindlessly," Nghiem admits. She bought coffee or bubble tea every morning and snacks in the afternoon. She also accumulated kitchen utensils even though they regularly ate out for lunch and dinner. Sang, meanwhile, spent heavily on social engagements he could have skipped. It is not uncommon for families with a large income to have poor savings. Some 61.4% of Vietnamese do not plan or manage their income and expenses, 53% say their families struggle to save, and 23.7% report not saving any money in the preceding 12 months, according to a 2022 survey by Japan International Cooperation Agency. Not being able to save reflects more than just income levels or spending habits, according to Nathan Gehlert, professor of psychology at Fulbright University Vietnam. One major factor is a lack of shared goals and concrete plans for reaching them, he says. Spouses can attach very different meanings to money, with one seeing it as a source of security and wanting to save and the other viewing it as a way to enjoy life, share with others or reward themselves, he explains. Rising incomes can also bring more expensive lifestyles and higher expectations, leaving little room for savings, he says. He advises couples to spend some time tracking and categorizing their expenses before agreeing on priorities, set personal spending allowances, and agree on a threshold for major purchases. Nghiem recalls somewhat guiltily that before they married, they earned only about VND10 million a month between them, rented modest accommodation, ate on the sidewalk, and had few expectations, but felt contented and happy. Their incomes rose after marriage, but disagreements followed, she laments. "When we had no money, we put our partner above everything else. Once we had money, we began prioritizing our own needs." Having to borrow for the house repairs prompted them to change their habits. They began allocating their monthly income: VND6 million–VND8 million for food, VND15 million for investments, VND10 million for emergencies, and another VND10 million for other living expenses. Nghiem bought ingredients to make drinks at home, sold kitchenware she did not need and began cooking more often. Sang turned down unnecessary social engagements. After eight months of saving and increasing their income, they were able to buy a car and had money when they needed. Ha and Peter also plan to manage their finances more systematically so they do not find themselves with a "zero-balance account" again. In the U.S., 39 states required personal finance education for high school graduation, according to the 2026 Council for Economic Education survey. Vietnam could learn from that model, Gehlert says.

picked.t: Dog meat in Singapore? Food agency investigates online sales
picked.body: Responding to queries on Thursday, SFA said it had not approved any source of dog meat and that all food imports must meet its requirements, according to The Straits Times. The statement followed a post on Wednesday in the Dogs Singapore Facebook group, which has since been deleted, alleged that an advertisement for dog meat dishes had appeared in a Vietnamese Facebook community group in Singapore. The advertisement reportedly used "Vitamin gau gau," slang commonly used in Vietnam to refer to dog meat, and claimed the meat was imported from Vietnam. The advertised dishes included grilled and steamed meats and ribs, with prices listed in Singapore dollars. Other Facebook posts appeared to show photos of meat cuts on display. SFA said meat and meat products may be imported only by licensed importers from sources accredited by the agency. Food brought in illegally from unknown sources can pose a food safety risk, it added. The agency urged importers and retailers to ensure that food products brought into Singapore for sale meet its import requirements and are safe to eat , Channel News Asia reported. Those convicted of selling meat or meat products without a valid license or import permit face a fine of up to SGD50,000 (US$39,000), imprisonment for up to two years, or both. Repeat offenders face a fine of up to SGD100,000, imprisonment for up to three years, or both.

picked.t: Dollar gains over dong on black market
picked.body: The greenback was up 0.31% to around VND25,930 at unofficial exchange points. The currency was steady at VND26,180 at lender Vietcombank. The State Bank of Vietnam hiked its reference rate by 0.02% to VND25,641. Globally, the dollar was set for its first back-to-back weekly gains in more than three months on Friday, as surging Treasury yields and mounting bets on further Federal ‌Reserve rate hikes kept the greenback near multi-month peaks, Reuters reported. The dollar index, which tracks the U.S. currency against a basket of peers, has risen more than 1% this week to a two-month high, marking its first back-to-back weekly gains since June. The rally was losing momentum, however, with the index last down slightly at 101.2. At 158.8 per dollar, the Japanese yen continued to hover near a three-week low. Dollar strength pushed the euro to a two-month low of $1.1370 and put it on track for a third weekly decline, its worst losing streak since the end of 2025. Sterling languished near a three-month low of $1.3220 and was on track for its worst weekly performance in four months.

picked.t: [뉴스로 보는 베트남어] 베트남 기업, 왜 글로벌 공급망에 깊이 못 들어갈까?
picked.body: (자료 제공=베트남어 배우기 오픈카카오톡 김기욱, ai활용 제작) 베트남의 무역 규모는 빠르게 성장하고 있지만, 국내 기업은 여전히 글로벌 공급망의 고부가가치 단계로 진입하는 데 어려움을 겪고 있다. 이러한 경제 현상과 관련된 뉴스 속 주요 베트남어 표현을 소개한다. Vì sao doanh nghiệp Việt khó tiến sâu vào chuỗi cung ứng toàn cầu?    왜 베트남 기업은 글로벌 공급망에 깊이 진입하기 어려운가?    핵심 단어 vì sao: 왜, 무슨 이유로    doanh nghiệp Việt: 베트남 기업    khó: 어렵다, ~하기 어렵다    tiến sâu vào: 깊이 진입하다, 더 깊숙이 들어가다    sâu: 깊은    chuỗi cung ứng: 공급망    toàn cầu: 전 세계의, 글로벌 베트남의 수출입 규모가 빠르게 커졌지만, 정작 베트남 내 기업들은 글로벌 공급망에서 고부가가치 단계로 충분히 올라가지 못하고 있다.  베트남의 수출액은 2021년 3,360억 달러에서 2025년 4,750억 달러로 증가했지만 국내 기업의 수출 비중은 같은 기간 26.4%에서 22.7%로 낮아졌다.  또한 글로벌 가치사슬에 참여하는 베트남 국내기업 비율도 2009년의 35%에서 2023년 18%로 감소했다.  전문가들은 문제의 핵심이 단순히 FDI 기업과 연결되는 데 있는 것이 아니라, 품질관리·생산성·기술·데이터 관리·납기 신뢰도·탄소배출·에너지 사용·노동조건·위험관리 등을 안정적으로 충족하면서 장기적인 공급관계를 유지할 역량이 부족하다는 데 있다고 지적했습니다.
